name: Simple Daily Breathing
description: A single daily breathing reset is enough to maintain a calm baseline and prevent stress from gradually building up.
research_basis: PSS stress maintenance; Preventive stress management
tutorial_steps: At a consistent time each day (morning coffee, lunch, before bed), take 5 slow deep belly breaths.
IN for 4 counts, OUT for 6 counts.
2-3 minutes total.
tips: Attaching this to an existing habit (coffee, commute, brushing teeth) ensures it actually happens.
video_title: Simple Breathing for Stress (YouTube)

name: Weekly Hobby Time
description: Low stress is best maintained by protecting time for activities that provide genuine enjoyment and psychological distance from responsibilities.
research_basis: Stress inoculation maintenance; Positive psychology leisure research
tutorial_steps: Identify one hobby or enjoyable activity you've been neglecting.
Schedule 30-60 minutes for it this week and put it in your calendar.
Protect this time like a meeting you can't cancel.
During the activity: be present — not thinking about your to-do list.
tips: Leisure is not a reward for finishing work. It's a requirement for sustainable performance.
video_title: Why Hobbies Are Essential for Stress (YouTube)

name: Scheduled Micro-Breaks
description: The brain works in 90-minute ultradian cycles. Taking 5-minute breaks at these natural intervals prevents stress from building and maintains cognitive performance.
research_basis: Ultradian rhythm research; Stress and recovery cycles (Peretz Lavie)
tutorial_steps: Set a recurring alarm for every 90 minutes during your work day.
When it goes off: stop, stand up, step away from your screen.
For 5 minutes: walk around, stretch, look out a window, make tea — anything non-screen.
Return to work.
tips: These breaks feel like a waste of time — they're not. They prevent the exhaustion that costs you 2 hours at the end of the day.
video_title: The Science of Taking Breaks (YouTube)

name: Box Breathing During Stress Breaks
description: Using Box Breathing during scheduled breaks transforms passive rest into active stress reduction, significantly lowering cumulative daily stress.
research_basis: PSS mild stress intervention; Sympathetic regulation during work stress
tutorial_steps: During any break, sit quietly and close your eyes.
Breathe IN for 4 counts, HOLD for 4, OUT for 4, HOLD for 4.
Repeat for 5-6 cycles (about 2 minutes).
Before returning to work: set one clear intention for the next 90 minutes.
tips: Even one round of box breathing during a stressful moment measurably reduces cortisol.
video_title: Box Breathing for Work Stress (YouTube)

name: Time Blocking
goals: Reduce overwhelm from too many tasks
description: Unstructured task lists increase stress because the brain constantly scans an open-ended threat. Assigning tasks to specific time blocks transforms an overwhelming list into a manageable schedule.
research_basis: Time management and PSS scores; Cognitive load reduction research
tutorial_steps: Each morning, take 10-15 minutes to review what needs to happen today.
Assign each task to a specific time block — not a list, but an actual calendar slot.
Include breaks in your blocking (e.g., 9-10:30 deep work, 10:30-10:45 break).
Be realistic — most people can do only 3-4 hours of deep work per day.
At end of day: what got done? Update tomorrow's blocks.
tips: The plan will change. That's okay. Having a plan and adapting it is far less stressful than having no plan.
video_title: Time Blocking — How to Manage Your Day (YouTube)

name: One Enjoyable Activity Daily
description: When under mild stress, people typically drop enjoyable activities first — creating a wellbeing deficit. Protecting one daily enjoyable activity maintains the stress buffer.
research_basis: Stress inoculation; Burnout prevention; Positive ratio (Fredrickson, 2001)
tutorial_steps: Each day, protect 15 minutes for something genuinely enjoyable — not productive, just enjoyable.
Examples: music, a walk, gaming, cooking something you like, reading for pleasure.
Schedule it at a specific time. Treat it as non-negotiable.
During it: actually be present.
tips: This is not self-indulgent. It is stress inoculation. People who burn out are the ones who drop enjoyment entirely.
video_title: Preventing Burnout — The Role of Enjoyment (YouTube)

name: Stress Trigger Log
description: Tracking when and why stress spikes occur reveals patterns invisible in the moment. Once patterns are identified, targeted interventions replace generic coping.
research_basis: Stress Inoculation Training (Meichenbaum, 1977); PSS clinical intervention
tutorial_steps: Each time stress spikes, write: Time, Situation, Stress 1-10, Physical sensation, Thought.
At end of each day: spend 2 minutes reviewing entries.
After one week: look for patterns — same times? Same people? Same situations?
Identify your top 2 stress triggers.
For each trigger: brainstorm one thing you could change or prepare.
tips: Stressed people often believe 'everything' causes stress. The log usually reveals it's 2-3 specific things.
video_title: Understanding Your Stress Triggers (YouTube)

name: Task Breakdown — Micro Steps
description: Overwhelming tasks trigger avoidance, which creates more stress. Breaking any task into tiny specific micro-steps eliminates the activation barrier.
research_basis: Implementation intention research (Gollwitzer, 1999); CBT for procrastination and stress
tutorial_steps: Write down the task that feels most overwhelming.
Ask: 'What is the absolute smallest first step?' (Not 'write the report' — but 'open a doc and type the title')
List 5 micro-steps from start to a defined stopping point.
Schedule step 1 with a specific time — max 15 minutes.
After step 1: celebrate it. Then assess: do step 2 now or later?
tips: Each step should feel almost too easy. That is intentional — it bypasses the brain's resistance to starting.
video_title: How to Break Tasks Down Under Stress (YouTube)

name: Evening Wind-Down Routine
description: Moderate stress leaves the nervous system activated well into the evening, impairing sleep and recovery. A structured wind-down routine signals the end of the stress period.
research_basis: Stress recovery research (Sonnentag & Fritz, 2007); CBT-I wind-down protocols
tutorial_steps: T-20 min: Dim all lights. Stop work-related activity completely.
T-15 min: Brain dump — write everything still on your mind for tomorrow.
T-10 min: Gentle stretching or light breathing (5 minutes).
T-5 min: Sit quietly with tea, calm music, or light reading.
Bedtime: 4-7-8 breathing for 2-3 cycles.
Keep this routine identical every night — consistency is what makes it work.
tips: Without a wind-down routine, under moderate stress your body stays in 'work mode' for hours after you stop working.
video_title: Evening Routine for Stress Recovery (YouTube)

name: Crisis Priority List
description: Under high stress overload, the first step is emergency triage — separating what MUST happen from everything else.
research_basis: Crisis management; Stress Inoculation Training high-stress protocol
tutorial_steps: Write every task and responsibility currently stressing you.
Mark each: CRITICAL / IMPORTANT / CAN WAIT / DELEGATE OR DROP.
Focus ONLY on CRITICAL items for the next 24 hours.
For each CRITICAL item: identify the single next action.
Do those actions only. Review the list tomorrow.
tips: At maximum stress, doing 3 critical things is better than attempting 15 everything.
video_title: How to Prioritize Under Extreme Stress (YouTube)

name: Delegation & Boundary Setting
description: High stress overload is often partly maintained by taking on responsibilities that can be delegated or declined.
research_basis: PSS high-stress clinical protocols; Assertiveness and stress research
tutorial_steps: From your task list: identify 2-3 things someone else could do.
Identify 1-2 commitments you need to decline or postpone.
For each delegation: identify who, and draft a clear direct ask.
For each boundary: decide what to say and say it — 'I can't take this on right now.'
This may feel uncomfortable. Do it anyway — your wellbeing depends on it.
tips: Delegation and boundaries are not failures — they're survival.
video_title: How to Delegate and Set Limits Under Stress (YouTube)

name: Finding Professional Stress Support
goals: Connect to professional support for severe stress
description: High stress overload that is persistent and unsustainable warrants professional support.
research_basis: Stress Inoculation Training professional referral; PSS high score protocols
tutorial_steps: Search for a therapist or counselor who specializes in stress or burnout.
Ask your doctor, HR, or check your insurance for referrals.
Look for professionals trained in CBT, ACT, or Stress Inoculation Training.
Make one contact today.
If cost is a barrier: check community mental health centers or online therapy platforms.
tips: Chronic high stress is a medical concern. Seeking help for it is as reasonable as seeing a doctor for physical pain.
video_title: When to Seek Help for Stress and Burnout (YouTube)

name: Maintain Sleep Schedule
description: Good sleep is maintained primarily through consistency. Protecting wake and sleep times keeps the circadian clock calibrated.
research_basis: Circadian biology; PSQI maintenance; CBT-I prevention
tutorial_steps: Keep your wake time within 30 minutes every day — including weekends.
Keep your bedtime within 30 minutes every day.
If you sleep in on weekends, do it by no more than 1 hour.
This is the single most impactful sleep habit to protect.
tips: Social jet lag (large weekend/weekday differences) is as harmful to energy as mild insomnia.
video_title: Sleep Schedule — Why Consistency Matters (YouTube)

name: Light Daily Movement
goals: Improve sleep quality through physical activity
description: Regular light movement significantly improves sleep quality. Consistency matters more than intensity.
research_basis: Exercise and sleep quality meta-analysis; PSQI physical activity correlation
tutorial_steps: Aim for 20-30 minutes of light movement daily — a walk, bike ride, or light workout.
Morning or afternoon is ideal — avoid vigorous exercise within 2 hours of bedtime.
Even 10-minute walks count.
Outdoor movement adds natural light exposure for circadian regulation.
tips: Even people who feel 'too tired to exercise' sleep better when they add light movement.
video_title: Exercise and Sleep — The Connection (YouTube)

name: Evening Routine Check
description: For good sleepers, a brief nightly check ensures protective habits stay in place.
research_basis: CBT-I sleep maintenance protocols
tutorial_steps: Each evening, do a quick 5-point check: screens off? Room cool and dark? Bedtime consistent? No caffeine after 2 PM? 10 min of something calming?
Fix any 'no' for tomorrow.
That's it.
tips: Good sleep hygiene erodes gradually — people stop noticing until quality is significantly worse.
video_title: Evening Routine for Better Sleep (YouTube)

name: Sleep Hygiene Basics
description: The core CBT-I sleep hygiene rules. The most evidence-based non-medication approach to improving sleep.
research_basis: CBT-I (Morin et al.); AASM Sleep Hygiene Guidelines; ISI clinical protocols
tutorial_steps: FIXED SCHEDULE: Same bedtime and wake time every day, including weekends.
BED = SLEEP ONLY: No work, eating, or screens in bed.
SCREENS OFF: No phone or laptop 45 minutes before bed.
COOL ROOM: 16-19°C / 60-67°F.
DARK ROOM: Blackout curtains or sleep mask.
CAFFEINE CUTOFF: Nothing caffeinated after 2 PM.
IF AWAKE 20+ MINUTES: Get up, calm activity in dim light, return when sleepy.
tips: Start with just ONE rule this week — the one you most consistently break.
video_title: Sleep Hygiene — CBT-I Basics (YouTube)

name: Screen Cutoff Rule
description: Blue light from screens delays melatonin onset by up to 2 hours. One of the highest-impact free sleep interventions.
research_basis: Harvard Medical School (Chang et al., 2015); Sleep Medicine Reviews
tutorial_steps: Set an alarm labeled 'SCREENS OFF' for 45 minutes before your bedtime.
When it goes off: put your phone in another room.
Use those 45 minutes for light reading, journaling, stretching, or quiet music.
Track sleep quality for 5 days — most people notice results within 3-5 nights.
tips: The dopamine loop of social media is also a problem — not just the blue light.
video_title: How Blue Light Affects Your Sleep (YouTube)

name: Morning Light Exposure
description: Bright natural light in the first 30 minutes of waking is the most powerful circadian clock signal. It also acts as a natural antidepressant with effect sizes comparable to medication.
research_basis: Circadian biology (Czeisler); Light therapy for depression (Terman, 2012); Huberman Lab
tutorial_steps: Within 30 minutes of waking: go outside or sit by a window with direct light.
Get 10 minutes of natural light on your face — no sunglasses if safe.
Overcast days still count — outdoor overcast light is brighter than indoor light.
Combine with something pleasant: coffee, a short walk, quiet time.
tips: Free, 10 minutes, improves both sleep and mood, backed by decades of circadian research. One of the highest-ROI health habits available.
video_title: Morning Sunlight for Sleep & Mood — Dr. Huberman (YouTube)

name: Sleep Schedule Builder
description: A core CBT-I technique. Choosing fixed sleep/wake times and adhering to them strictly for 3 weeks rebuilds the circadian signal.
research_basis: CBT-I sleep restriction and scheduling (Morin, 1993); Stimulus control therapy
tutorial_steps: Choose a wake time you can commit to 7 days a week (e.g., 7:00 AM).
Count back 7.5-8 hours for your target bedtime (e.g., 11:00 PM).
Week 1: only go to bed when genuinely sleepy AND past your target bedtime.
Wake at your fixed time NO MATTER WHAT — even after a bad night.
No naps longer than 20 minutes during this phase.
After 2 weeks of consistency: assess and adjust if needed.
tips: The first 2-3 days may feel harder. That's normal — you're building sleep pressure. It gets significantly better by week 2.
video_title: CBT-I Sleep Schedule Rebuilding (YouTube)

name: Caffeine Audit & Tracking
description: Caffeine has a 5-6 hour half-life. A 3 PM coffee still has 50% active at 9 PM. Many people don't realize their sleep problems are caffeine-driven.
research_basis: Caffeine metabolism research; PSQI caffeine correlation
tutorial_steps: For one week, log every caffeinated item: time, what, how much.
Includes: coffee, tea, energy drinks, pre-workout, some medications.
Identify your last caffeine intake each day and the time you had trouble sleeping.
Move your caffeine cutoff earlier by 1 hour and observe for 3 days.
Target: no caffeine after 1-2 PM for most people.
tips: Caffeine sensitivity varies widely. Track to find YOUR personal cutoff.
video_title: Caffeine and Sleep — What You Need to Know (YouTube)

name: Pre-Sleep Wind-Down Routine
goals: Signal the brain sleep is coming
description: The brain needs 20-30 minutes to downshift from waking alertness to sleep. This structured routine creates consistent signals that sleep is coming.
research_basis: CBT-I sleep onset protocol; Sleep onset latency research
tutorial_steps: T-20 min: Dim all lights.
T-15 min: Brain dump — write tomorrow's to-do list and any lingering thoughts.
T-10 min: Light stretching or 5-minute PMR.
T-5 min: Sit in bed with a physical book or just quiet.
Lying down: 4-7-8 breathing for 2-3 cycles.
Keep the routine identical every night — the ritual becomes the sleep cue.
tips: Think of it like a baby's bedtime routine — the sequence itself becomes the signal for sleep.
video_title: Build a Wind-Down Routine for Better Sleep (YouTube)

name: Sleep Tracking Log
description: For severe sleep problems, tracking provides the data needed to identify what's disrupting sleep. Used as a standard tool in CBT-I clinical programs.
research_basis: CBT-I sleep diary (Morin, 1993); ISI tracking protocols
tutorial_steps: Every morning within 15 minutes of waking, log: bedtime, estimated sleep onset time, number of awakenings, final wake time, total sleep estimate, mood/energy on waking (1-10).
Don't check the clock at night — estimates only. Clock-watching worsens insomnia.
After 2 weeks: review for your 2-3 biggest disruptors.
Use the log to track change as you implement sleep interventions.
tips: Estimates are fine. The patterns across 14 days reveal what the brain can't notice night to night.
video_title: How to Use a Sleep Diary (YouTube)

name: Sleep Recovery Plan
goals: Structured recovery from severe insomnia or fatigue
description: A structured multi-week plan combining all evidence-based sleep interventions for severe sleep problems. CBT-I has a 70-80% success rate for chronic insomnia.
research_basis: CBT-I full protocol (Morin, 1993; Harvey, 2007); ISI severe remission pathway
tutorial_steps: WEEK 1: Fix wake time only. Wake at the same time every day no matter what.
WEEK 2: Add caffeine cutoff (1-2 PM) and screen cutoff (45 min before bed).
WEEK 3: Add pre-sleep wind-down routine and bedroom environment improvements.
WEEK 4: Add stimulus control — bed for sleep only; get up if awake 20+ minutes.
Throughout: keep sleep tracking log. Review weekly.
After 4 weeks: assess with a healthcare provider if severe symptoms persist.
tips: CBT-I has better long-term outcomes than sleep medication. Give it 4 weeks.
video_title: CBT-I — The Complete Sleep Recovery Protocol (YouTube)

name: Medical Sleep Evaluation
goals: Rule out medical causes of severe sleep problems
description: Severe sleep problems may have underlying medical causes (sleep apnea, restless legs, thyroid) that behavioral interventions alone cannot address.
research_basis: Sleep medicine clinical guidelines; AASM referral criteria
tutorial_steps: Contact your doctor and describe your sleep symptoms: how long, what type (can't fall asleep / wake frequently / never feel rested).
Ask specifically about a sleep study if you snore heavily, wake gasping, or feel exhausted despite adequate time in bed.
Also ask about thyroid function and iron levels — both affect sleep quality.
Bring your sleep tracking log if you have one.
tips: Sleep apnea affects roughly 1 in 5 adults and is significantly underdiagnosed. If you snore and feel unrefreshed, ask specifically about it.
video_title: When to See a Doctor for Sleep Problems (YouTube)

name: Contact One Trusted Person
description: Severe loneliness requires immediate action. This exercise identifies and activates even one existing support connection as a first step out of isolation.
research_basis: UCLA Loneliness Scale interventions; Crisis social support research
tutorial_steps: Think of the ONE person in your life you trust most — even if you haven't spoken in a while.
Contact them today: 'Hey, I've been having a hard time. Can we talk?'
You don't have to explain everything. Just opening a line of contact is the first step.
If there is truly no one: contact a support line (findahelpline.com).
Notice how it felt vs. the isolation of not contacting.
tips: Severe loneliness tells you no one cares. This is the loneliness talking, not reality. Test it.
video_title: Breaking Isolation — How to Reach Out (YouTube)

name: Online Support Groups
goals: Find community when local connection is difficult
description: When in-person social connection is unavailable, online communities provide genuine belonging and understanding that directly reduces loneliness.
research_basis: Online social support and loneliness research; UCLA Loneliness Scale digital interventions
tutorial_steps: Identify one area of interest, challenge, or experience you have.
Search for online communities: Reddit, Discord, Facebook Groups, topic-specific forums.
Start by reading — you don't have to post right away.
When ready: make one comment or introduction post.
Engage 3-4 times per week for 2 weeks and assess how it feels.
tips: Choose communities that feel supportive, not ones that amplify distress. Quality matters more than quantity.
video_title: Finding Community Online for Mental Health (YouTube)

name: Crisis Support Line
goals: Immediate human contact for isolation or crisis
description: When severely alone or in emotional crisis, crisis lines provide immediate human connection with trained listeners — confidential and free.
research_basis: Crisis intervention; Social support emergency protocols
tutorial_steps: Egypt: 08008880700 (mental health support line).
International directory: findahelpline.com
Text-based options exist if calling feels too hard.
You don't need to be suicidal to call — severe loneliness and distress are valid reasons.
They are trained to listen without judgment.
tips: 'I feel very alone and just need to talk to someone' is a completely valid reason to call.
video_title: How to Use a Support Helpline (YouTube)

name: Text One Friend This Week
description: Moderate loneliness is reduced most effectively by small, low-barrier social actions. Texting one person is the minimum viable social act.
research_basis: UCLA Loneliness Scale; Behavioral Activation social component
tutorial_steps: Think of one friend or acquaintance you'd like to reconnect with.
Send one text: 'Hey, I was thinking about you. How are you doing?'
No need for a long conversation.
If they reply: respond. If not: try someone else next time.
Did you feel slightly less alone after sending it?
tips: A 3-sentence exchange still counts as social contact.
video_title: Small Steps to Reduce Loneliness (YouTube)

name: Join an Online Community
goals: Find shared interests and reduce isolation
description: Finding a community around a shared interest provides social belonging without the pressure of one-on-one interaction.
research_basis: Social belonging research; Online community and loneliness (Cacioppo, 2008)
tutorial_steps: Think of any interest, hobby, or experience that defines you.
Search for an online community around it (Reddit, Discord, Facebook Groups, forums).
Join and browse for a week before participating.
Make one comment or question — keep it genuine.
Return weekly and gradually become a regular presence.
tips: Shared interest communities feel less vulnerable than general social spaces.
video_title: Building Connection Through Shared Interests (YouTube)

name: Find a Local or Online Interest Group
goals: Build new social connections through shared activities
description: Structured group activities around shared interests provide natural social connection without the pressure of starting conversations from scratch.
research_basis: Social activity and loneliness (UCLA scale); Community belonging research
tutorial_steps: Identify one activity you enjoy or are curious about.
Search: Meetup.com, Facebook Events, local clubs, sports teams, volunteering organizations, or classes.
Commit to attending once. Tell yourself: I only have to try this once.
At the event: one small conversation is enough.
If it felt okay: go again. Repeated attendance builds familiarity, which builds connection.
tips: You don't have to like everyone or feel instantly connected. Familiarity builds connection gradually.
video_title: Making New Friends as an Adult (YouTube)

name: Maintain Regular Contact
description: Good social connections require consistent maintenance. Regular small check-ins keep relationships strong.
research_basis: Relationship quality and mental health; UCLA Loneliness Scale healthy social practices
tutorial_steps: Identify 3-5 people you value in your life.
Set a goal to have a brief meaningful contact with at least one every 2-3 days.
This can be: a text, a voice note, a call, something genuine.
Quality beats quantity. One specific thoughtful message matters more than five generic ones.
tips: Strong relationships don't maintain themselves. They need regular small investments — just like plants need water.
video_title: How to Maintain Strong Friendships (YouTube)

name: Weekly Social Activity
description: People with good social support who maintain regular social activities have significantly better mental health outcomes.
research_basis: Social activity and mental health; UCLA Loneliness Scale proactive practices
tutorial_steps: Schedule one social activity per week — coffee, dinner, a sport, a walk, a shared activity.
Plan it in advance — spontaneous activities are great but unreliable.
Diversify across different relationships over time.
After each activity: what did you enjoy? Who do you want to see more?
tips: Consistent weekly social investment is one of the strongest predictors of long-term life satisfaction.
video_title: Social Connection and Mental Health (YouTube)

name: Express Gratitude to Someone
description: Expressing specific appreciation to people in your life deepens bonds and increases wellbeing for both sender and receiver.
research_basis: Seligman et al. (2005) gratitude expression; Social bond research; Positive psychology
tutorial_steps: Think of someone who did something meaningful for you — recently or long ago.
Write or say specifically what they did AND how it affected you.
Format: 'When you [specific action], it made me feel [specific feeling]. It really mattered.'
Deliver it — text, call, or in person.
Notice both their reaction and yours.
tips: Specific beats general. 'You're a great friend' is nice. 'When you called to check on me last month, it meant everything' — that's connection.
video_title: The Power of Expressing Gratitude (YouTube)

name: Deepen Existing Connections
goals: Move from surface-level to meaningful relationships
description: Strong social support is most protective when relationships are deep, not just numerous.
research_basis: Relationship depth and wellbeing; Intimacy research (Reis & Shaver, 1988)
tutorial_steps: Identify 1-2 relationships you want to deepen.
Plan one deeper interaction: share something real about yourself, ask meaningful questions.
Good questions: 'What's something you're excited about?', 'What's been weighing on you?', 'What was the best moment of your week?'
Be willing to be vulnerable — depth requires reciprocal openness.
tips: Consistent genuine interest and occasional real sharing are what build deep bonds.
video_title: How to Have Deeper Conversations (YouTube)

name: Practice Reciprocal Support
description: Giving support to others has as large a wellbeing benefit as receiving it. Reciprocal relationships are more stable and more protective for mental health.
research_basis: Giving and wellbeing research; Social support reciprocity
tutorial_steps: Think of someone in your life who might be struggling right now.
Reach out with genuine support: 'I was thinking about you. How are you really doing?'
Listen fully — don't try to fix unless asked. Just listen.
Follow up in a few days.
Notice how giving support makes you feel.
tips: People with strong support networks both give AND receive — it's not one-directional.
video_title: Giving Support — The Wellbeing Benefits (YouTube)

name: Community Involvement
goals: Build sense of purpose and belonging through contributing to something larger
description: Participation in community — volunteering, local groups, collective activities — provides one of the deepest forms of social belonging and purpose.
research_basis: Community involvement and wellbeing; Purpose and mental health (Frankl; Ryff, 1989)
tutorial_steps: Identify one cause, community, or group you care about.
Find a concrete way to participate: volunteer event, local club, community clean-up, advocacy organization.
Commit to attending once and assessing.
If it resonated: commit to regular participation.
Reflect: does contributing to something beyond yourself affect how you feel?
tips: Volunteering has one of the strongest evidence bases for wellbeing of any behavioral intervention.
video_title: Why Community Involvement Improves Mental Health (YouTube)
